title: Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate
summary: A finished income property is worth its net operating income divided by the market cap rate. Yield on cost uses the same NOI against what it cost you to build, and the two numbers are the start of every development decision.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a completed building is valued by its income, not by what it cost to build. Take the yearly net operating income, divide by the market cap rate, and you have the value a buyer or a lender will recognise.

The idea

Every income property throws off a stream of cash. Investors price that stream the way you would price a bond: they decide what yearly return they need, and the price is whatever makes the income equal that return. That yearly return is called the capitalisation rate, or cap rate.

The income in question is net operating income, NOI. It is rent and other income actually collected, minus the costs of running the building: property tax, insurance, repairs, management, utilities the landlord pays. NOI deliberately leaves out three things: loan interest and principal (that is how one particular owner financed it, not what the building earns), depreciation (an accounting entry, not cash), and income tax.

  • Cap rate = NOI divided by value. Units: percent per year.
  • Value = NOI divided by the cap rate. Units: dollars.
  • Yield on cost = stabilised NOI divided by total development cost. Units: percent per year.

Cap rate and yield on cost use the same NOI. The difference is the denominator: the market's price on one side, your all-in cost on the other. Week 1 is about the gap between them.

Worked example. A hypothetical 40-apartment building rents each unit for 2,000 dollars a month.

  1. Gross potential rent: 40 units times 2,000 dollars times 12 months = 960,000 dollars a year.
  2. Vacancy and bad debt of 5 percent: 5 percent of 960,000 = 48,000 dollars. Effective income = 912,000 dollars.
  3. Operating expenses of 312,000 dollars a year. NOI = 912,000 minus 312,000 = 600,000 dollars.
  4. Comparable buildings trade at a 6 percent cap rate. Value = 600,000 divided by 0.06 = 10 million dollars.
  5. If it cost 8 million dollars all-in to build, yield on cost = 600,000 divided by 8 million = 7.5 percent.

Now the part that matters for risk. Suppose buyers demand a 6.5 percent cap rate instead of 6. Value = 600,000 divided by 0.065 = about 9.23 million dollars. Half a percentage point on the cap rate wiped out about 770,000 dollars, nearly 8 percent of the value, and the building did not change at all. Because the cap rate sits in the denominator, small moves in it produce large moves in value, and the lower the cap rate, the bigger the swing.

Two habits to build. First, always ask which NOI you are looking at: in-place today, or a projection after you finish and lease up. Second, always ask where the cap rate came from: recent comparable sales, or someone's hope.

Tonight's drill

Three problems. Try each before you open the answer.

Problem 1

A building earns NOI of 450,000 dollars a year. What is it worth at a 5 percent cap rate? What is it worth at a 6 percent cap rate? How much value is lost, in dollars and as a percentage?

Problem 2

A hypothetical retail building you are about to complete will bill 1.2 million dollars of rent a year. You expect 10 percent vacancy and credit loss. Operating expenses are 380,000 dollars. The loan will cost 300,000 dollars of interest a year, and the accountant will book 150,000 dollars of depreciation. It cost 10 million dollars to build, and similar buildings trade at a 5.6 percent cap rate. Find the NOI, the yield on cost, and the value.

Problem 3

A developer hands a lender a one-page summary: stabilised NOI of 700,000 dollars, a 5.6 percent cap rate, value 12.5 million dollars. What would a lender ask before believing that value?

The roommate question

In grid reliability you never trust one operating point; you ask what happens when an assumption moves. Which single input in today's formula behaves most like a line rating that everyone quietly treats as fixed, and how would you test it the way you test N-1?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. At 5 percent: 450,000 divided by 0.05 = 9 million dollars.
  2. At 6 percent: 450,000 divided by 0.06 = 7.5 million dollars.
  3. Loss: 9 million minus 7.5 million = 1.5 million dollars. As a percentage of the starting value: 1.5 divided by 9 = about 16.7 percent.

Usual error: thinking one percentage point on the cap rate means about one percent of value. The cap rate is the denominator, so going from 5 to 6 is a 20 percent rise in the rate and cuts value by about a sixth.

Rule: value moves inversely with the cap rate, and the lower the cap rate the harder a small change bites.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Vacancy and credit loss: 10 percent of 1.2 million = 120,000 dollars. Effective income = 1,080,000 dollars.
  2. NOI = 1,080,000 minus 380,000 operating expenses = 700,000 dollars. Interest and depreciation are not deducted.
  3. Yield on cost = 700,000 divided by 10 million = 7 percent.
  4. Value = 700,000 divided by 0.056 = 12.5 million dollars.

Usual error: subtracting the 300,000 of interest and the 150,000 of depreciation, which gives a "NOI" of 250,000 and a value of about 4.5 million dollars. Interest belongs to this owner's financing and depreciation is an accounting entry; neither is a cost of operating the building.

Rule: NOI stops above the financing line; interest, principal, depreciation and income tax come later.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
A lender would want each input proved, roughly in this order:

  • The rent: is the 700,000 based on signed leases or projected market rent? Show the rent roll or the comparable rents.
  • The vacancy and expenses: are they realistic for this type and area? A low expense ratio is a classic way to inflate NOI. Has property tax been set on the new, higher assessed value?
  • The cap rate: which recent sales support 5.6 percent, and how similar were they? What is the value at 6.5 percent? (About 10.8 million dollars.)
  • Independence: the lender will order its own appraisal and lend on the lower of cost-based and value-based tests, not on the developer's page.

Usual error: treating the value as a fact. It is two estimates divided by each other.

Rule: a value is only as good as the NOI evidence and the cap rate evidence behind it.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
The cap rate is the line rating everyone treats as fixed. It is set by the market, it moves without asking you, and the whole valuation hangs on it. In N-1 you take the system as planned, remove the largest single element, and check it still holds. The development equivalent is to take your plan, move the cap rate by the biggest credible amount, say half to one full percentage point, and check the deal still works.

The difference worth noticing: on the grid you design to survive the contingency outright. In development you are deciding how much of a swing you can absorb before your profit disappears, so you want to know the breakpoint, not just a pass or fail.

Rule: never accept a value without asking what it becomes when the cap rate moves.

rule: Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate, and NOI never includes debt, depreciation or income tax.

title: Development spread and profit on cost
summary: The development spread is the gap between your yield on cost and the market cap rate, and it is what creates the profit. Profit on cost turns that gap into dollars and a percentage you can compare across deals.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a development makes money only if it produces income more cheaply than the market will pay for that income. The spread between yield on cost and the cap rate is that cheapness, and profit on cost is how big it is in dollars.

The idea

Yesterday you met two rates built on the same NOI. Yield on cost divides NOI by what you spent. The cap rate divides NOI by what a buyer will pay. If you can build a stream of income at a 7 percent yield and the market will buy it at a 5.6 percent cap rate, you have manufactured value: the buyer pays more for the income than it cost you to create it.

  • Development spread = yield on cost minus market cap rate. Units: percentage points, usually quoted in basis points (100 basis points = 1 percentage point).
  • Profit = completed value minus total development cost. Units: dollars.
  • Profit on cost = profit divided by total development cost. Units: percent.
  • Profit on value, also called margin = profit divided by completed value. Same profit, smaller percentage. Always check which one someone is quoting.

One shortcut ties them together: profit on cost = yield on cost divided by cap rate, minus 1. It shows that profit depends on the ratio of the two rates, not on the size of the building.

Worked example. A hypothetical apartment project will cost 20 million dollars all-in, including land, construction, fees and financing. Once leased, it will earn NOI of 1.4 million dollars a year. Comparable buildings trade at a 5.6 percent cap rate.

  1. Yield on cost = 1.4 million divided by 20 million = 7.0 percent.
  2. Spread = 7.0 minus 5.6 = 1.4 percentage points, which is 140 basis points.
  3. Value = 1.4 million divided by 0.056 = 25 million dollars.
  4. Profit = 25 million minus 20 million = 5 million dollars.
  5. Profit on cost = 5 divided by 20 = 25 percent. Check with the shortcut: 7.0 divided by 5.6 = 1.25, minus 1 = 25 percent.
  6. Profit on value = 5 divided by 25 = 20 percent.

Why it matters: the spread is your entire cushion. Every risk in development, a cost overrun, slower leasing, a higher cap rate when you finish, eats into it from one side or the other. A cost overrun lowers your yield on cost; a market shift raises the cap rate. Both narrow the spread at the same time in a bad year.

Many developers use rules of thumb such as wanting at least 100 to 200 basis points of spread, or a profit on cost in the mid-teens or higher, before taking construction risk. Those are market habits that shift with interest rates and project risk, not fixed laws, and a riskier project should demand a wider cushion.

One last caution: the cap rate that counts is the one the market will apply when you finish, often two or three years away, not today's. Professionals call it the exit cap rate and usually set it a little higher than today's to be safe.

Tonight's drill

Three problems, each building on the last.

Problem 1

A project costs 30 million dollars all-in and will earn stabilised NOI of 2.1 million dollars. The market cap rate is 6 percent. Find the yield on cost, the spread in basis points, the completed value, the profit and the profit on cost.

Problem 2

Same project, but things go wrong together: costs overrun by 10 percent, and by completion the cap rate has moved to 6.5 percent. NOI is unchanged. Recalculate the yield on cost, the spread, the value and the profit.

Problem 3

A developer pitches a lender the original plan from Problem 1, with its 100 basis point spread. What would a lender ask to judge whether that cushion is wide enough?

The roommate question

The development spread is a margin between what you deliver and what you need. Where do you work with a margin like that, and what does Problem 2 have in common with two contingencies arriving at once?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Yield on cost = 2.1 million divided by 30 million = 7 percent.
  2. Spread = 7 minus 6 = 1 percentage point = 100 basis points.
  3. Value = 2.1 million divided by 0.06 = 35 million dollars.
  4. Profit = 35 million minus 30 million = 5 million dollars.
  5. Profit on cost = 5 divided by 30 = about 16.7 percent. Shortcut check: 7 divided by 6 = 1.167, minus 1 = 16.7 percent.

Usual error: quoting profit on value (5 divided by 35, about 14.3 percent) as if it were profit on cost. Both are legitimate; mixing them makes two deals look different when they are not.

Rule: always say which denominator a profit percentage uses.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. New cost = 30 million times 1.10 = 33 million dollars.
  2. Yield on cost = 2.1 million divided by 33 million = about 6.36 percent.
  3. Spread = 6.36 minus 6.5 = about minus 0.14 percentage points, or minus 14 basis points. The spread has gone negative.
  4. Value = 2.1 million divided by 0.065 = about 32.31 million dollars.
  5. Profit = 32.31 million minus 33 million = a loss of about 690,000 dollars, roughly minus 2.1 percent on cost.

Usual error: testing each shock alone. The overrun alone leaves a 2 million dollar profit; the cap rate move alone leaves about 2.3 million. Together they turn a 5 million dollar profit into a loss, because one shrinks the yield and the other raises the bar at the same time.

Rule: a 100 basis point spread can vanish from two ordinary problems arriving together.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• Cost certainty: is the construction price fixed or open-ended? How much contingency is in the 30 million, and how complete is the design?
  • Rent evidence: what supports 2.1 million of NOI? Signed pre-leases, or market surveys?
  • Exit cap rate: why 6 percent at completion? What happens at 6.5 or 7?
  • Time: how long to build and lease up, and what does a six-month delay cost in interest?
  • Equity: how much of the developer's own money is in first, and is it real cash or a land value someone appraised?

Usual error: defending the spread with the projected numbers themselves. The lender's question is how much each input could move.

Rule: a thin spread is acceptable only when the inputs behind it are nearly certain.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
It is your operating reserve or transfer margin: the gap between what the system can deliver and what it must carry. A healthy margin covers one credible event. Problem 2 is the equivalent of losing a large generator while a major line is out: each event alone is survivable, but planning only for single events understates the risk when causes are linked. In development they often are linked, because the same weak economy that pushes cap rates up also delays leasing and strains contractors.

Rule: size the spread for the correlated bad case, not for one problem at a time.

rule: Profit comes from the spread between yield on cost and the cap rate, and that spread is the whole cushion against every risk.

title: Residual land value: what you can afford to pay
summary: Residual land value works backwards from the finished value to the most you can pay for the land and still earn your target profit. Because land is what is left over, it swings much harder than any other number in the deal.
body:
Mr Shabazz, land is worth what is left after you pay for everything else and keep the profit you need. Work backwards from the finished value, and you know the ceiling on your land bid before you fall in love with a site.

The idea

Sellers price land by comparison and by hope. A developer has a better tool: start with what the finished building will be worth, subtract every cost of producing it, subtract the profit you require for the risk, and the remainder is the most the land can be worth to you. That remainder is the residual land value.

The trap is the profit. If your target is a profit on cost, and land is itself a cost, then the profit depends on the land price you are trying to find. The clean way round it:

  • Completed value = stabilised NOI divided by exit cap rate. Units: dollars.
  • Maximum total cost = completed value divided by (1 plus target profit on cost). Units: dollars.
  • Residual land value = maximum total cost minus all costs other than land. Units: dollars.

If instead your target is a margin on value, the profit is simply that percentage of the completed value, and land = value minus other costs minus profit. The two methods give different answers, so know which one your target uses.

Worked example. A hypothetical site would support a building with stabilised NOI of 1.38 million dollars. The exit cap rate is 6 percent. All costs other than land, meaning construction, soft costs, contingency and financing, total 16.5 million dollars. You require a 15 percent profit on cost.

  1. Completed value = 1.38 million divided by 0.06 = 23 million dollars.
  2. Maximum total cost = 23 million divided by 1.15 = 20 million dollars.
  3. Residual land value = 20 million minus 16.5 million = 3.5 million dollars.
  4. Check: total cost 20 million, value 23 million, profit 3 million, and 3 divided by 20 = 15 percent. It works.

Compare the common shortcut: take 15 percent of the 16.5 million of other costs (about 2.48 million) as profit, giving land of about 4.03 million dollars. That overpays, because it forgets that the land needs to earn a profit too. Paying 4.03 million would leave a profit on cost of only about 12.1 percent.

Now the property that makes land dangerous. The residual is a small number left over after subtracting two large ones. If the completed value falls 5 percent, to 21.85 million, the maximum total cost falls to 19 million, and land falls to 2.5 million dollars: down almost 29 percent. Engineers would call this gearing. A small error in value or cost becomes a large error in what the land is worth.

Two practical notes. The land price also carries closing costs and holding costs, such as interest and property tax until construction starts, so leave room for them. And a seller's asking price is just an opening position; your residual is the number that tells you when to walk away.

Tonight's drill

The second problem is the one that teaches the most.

Problem 1

A completed project will be worth 18 million dollars. All costs other than land total 12 million dollars. You require a 20 percent profit on cost. What is the most you can pay for the land?

Problem 2

A site supports stabilised NOI of 1.17 million dollars. All costs other than land are 13.8 million dollars and you require 15 percent profit on cost. Find the residual land value at a 6.5 percent exit cap rate, then again at 7 percent. By what percentage does the land value fall?

Problem 3

Use Problem 1. The seller insists on 4 million dollars for the land, a million above your residual. What profit on cost would you earn if you paid it, and what would a lender ask if you went ahead?

The roommate question

Residual land value is what is left after every fixed commitment and a required margin are subtracted from a total. Which transmission capability calculation has exactly that shape, and why does the leftover swing so much?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Maximum total cost = 18 million divided by 1.20 = 15 million dollars.
  2. Residual land value = 15 million minus 12 million = 3 million dollars.
  3. Check: profit = 18 minus 15 = 3 million, and 3 divided by 15 = 20 percent.

Usual error: taking 20 percent of the 12 million of other costs (2.4 million) as the profit and paying 3.6 million for the land. That leaves only 2.4 million of profit on a 15.6 million cost, about 15.4 percent, because the land itself earned nothing.

Rule: divide the value by one plus the target to find the cost ceiling, then subtract.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. At 6.5 percent: value = 1.17 million divided by 0.065 = 18 million dollars. Maximum total cost = 18 million divided by 1.15 = about 15.65 million. Land = 15.65 minus 13.8 = about 1.85 million dollars.
  2. At 7 percent: value = 1.17 million divided by 0.07 = about 16.71 million dollars. Maximum total cost = 16.71 divided by 1.15 = about 14.53 million. Land = 14.53 minus 13.8 = about 730,000 dollars.
  3. Fall in land value: from about 1.85 million to about 0.73 million, a drop of about 1.12 million, or roughly 60 percent.

The value fell only about 7 percent, but the land fell about 60 percent.

Usual error: assuming land moves in proportion to building value. It does not; the fixed 13.8 million of other costs stays put, so the whole loss lands on the residual.

Rule: the residual is geared, so stress it hardest of all.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
1. Total cost = 12 million plus 4 million = 16 million dollars.
  2. Profit = 18 million minus 16 million = 2 million dollars.
  3. Profit on cost = 2 divided by 16 = 12.5 percent, against your 20 percent target.

A lender would ask: what is the land worth on an independent appraisal, and will they count it at the price paid or at that lower value in the loan-to-cost test? Where is the extra million coming from, the developer's cash or more debt? Is there a credible reason value will be higher, such as more density from a rezoning, and is that already approved? A lender usually wants the developer's own equity to absorb an overpayment, not the loan.

Usual error: believing a great building will rescue a high land price. It cannot; the overpayment comes straight out of profit.

Rule: your residual is your walk-away price, not your opening offer.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
Available transfer capability has the same structure: total transfer capability, minus the reliability margin, minus the capacity benefit margin, minus existing commitments. Like land, it is the leftover after large quantities are subtracted, so a modest drop in the total, from a line out of service or a lower thermal limit in hot weather, can wipe out most of what is available. The required profit plays the role of the reliability margin: it is held back first and is not up for negotiation.

Rule: whenever a number is a small difference between large ones, expect it to swing hard.

rule: Land is the residual: value divided by one plus your target, minus every other cost, and it swings harder than anything else.
